strengths: Well-motivated and clearly written paper addressing a real and practical problem: label noise in preference datasets for LLM alignment.

Principled technical contribution: the EM formulation treating label correctness as a latent variable, and the general probabilistic bridge (Eq. 2) that converts arbitrary preference losses (DPO, IPO, SimPO, CPO) into posterior probabilities, elevating the method to a general 'meta-framework' rather than a single algorithm.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: four alignment algorithm families, two backbones, AlpacaEval 2 and Arena-Hard, plus a real multi-annotator dataset (MultiPref) with 227 annotators where the per-annotator reliability modeling is genuinely exercised.
Comparison against relevant robustness baselines (label smoothing, rDPO, Hölder-DPO) rather than only vanilla methods, and RE-PO is generally best-in-family.

Includes a convergence theorem with a clean proof (strict concavity of the reliability log-likelihood) and, notably, a dedicated controlled experiment (Section 5.5, Figure 2) that empirically verifies the reliability-estimation behavior under synthetic noise—a nice theory-to-practice loop.

Useful additional analyses: hyperparameter ablations (η0, EMA α), per-annotator reliability histograms robust to prior choice, judge-model robustness check (Appendix G), runtime overhead analysis (Appendix H), and qualitative case studies of down-weighted noisy labels.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the core mechanism—EM over latent label correctness with annotator reliability—is a direct application of the classic Dawid–Skene / Crowd-BT lineage, and ROPO [Liang et al., 2024] already performs iterative down-weighting of uncertain samples for preference optimization. ROPO is discussed as 'complementary' but not empirically compared, which weakens the claimed advantage over the closest prior work.

The main experiments (Table 2) use UltraFeedback-based datasets with a single 'virtual annotator' (K=1), where η collapses to a global scalar and RE-PO reduces to per-sample re-weighting driven by the model's own confidence. This creates a potential confirmation-bias/circularity concern: the model may down-weight labels that legitimately disagree with its evolving preferences, conflating preference diversity with label noise. The MultiPref experiments partially mitigate this but only for the DPO family.

The theoretical guarantee (Theorem 4.1) rests on a perfectly calibrated model—essentially assuming the model already matches the ground-truth preference distribution—which substantially limits its practical relevance; the authors honestly acknowledge this, but the theory is then more intuition than guarantee.

Results are not uniformly favorable: label smoothing sometimes beats RE-PO (e.g., SimPO w/ LS at 48.1 LC vs. 46.9 for RE-PO on Llama-3-8B), suggesting part of the gain may come from generic regularization rather than explicit noise modeling; the text slightly overstates consistency.

No variance/significance reporting for the main results (Table 2); gains of 1–3 points in several cells may not be statistically distinguishable, and AlpacaEval 2 / Arena-Hard LLM-judge evaluations are known to be noisy. No human evaluation.
Evaluation scope is limited to 7B–8B instruction-tuned models and two benchmark families; scalability of the reliability estimation to larger models or multi-turn settings is untested.
Missing standard deviation across seeds for the main table makes the reproducibility of the exact improvements harder to assess, and code release is not mentioned.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem (label noise in preference data) and the proposed EM-based reweighting is clearly described and easy to follow.

The evaluation is broad in scope: four alignment objectives (DPO, IPO, SimPO, CPO), two backbones, a real multi-annotator dataset (MultiPref), robustness baselines (rDPO, Hölder-DPO, label smoothing), ablations, a judge-model robustness check, and a runtime overhead analysis.

The theoretical derivation connecting preference losses to a probabilistic model (Appendix A/B) is clean, and the controlled synthetic-noise experiments in Section 5.5 empirically verify the reliability-estimation claim.
Reproducibility materials are reasonable: models, datasets, and hardware/hyperparameter details are documented in the appendix.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core method is a fairly direct application of Dawid–Skene/Crowd-BT-style EM label-reliability estimation to DPO-family losses. Given existing robust-alignment work (ROPO, rDPO, Hölder-DPO, Selective DPO), the contribution is incremental, and the 'general framework' framing overstates a straightforward soft-label construction.

The main experiments do not actually test the motivating claim. UltraFeedback-based datasets (K=1, single virtual annotator) are largely clean, GPT-4-derived data, yet the largest gains (+7 LC) are reported there. This raises the concern that the improvements stem from a generic regularization/label-smoothing effect rather than from noise mitigation — the very mechanism the paper claims as its core contribution. Stronger evidence would require experiments on datasets with known injected noise at the main scale.

The theoretical guarantee (Theorem 4.1) is weak and nearly trivial: it assumes a perfectly calibrated model with known ground-truth preference probabilities, fixed p*_i, and full-batch EM — conditions that contradict the setting the method is intended for (the model is being trained and is initially miscalibrated). The mini-batch EMA implementation breaks all EM guarantees, so the theorem provides little support for the practical algorithm.

A self-reinforcing-loop concern is not analyzed: the E-step computes label confidence from the model's own current preference probabilities, so 'noisy' labels are identified as those the model disagrees with. Downweighting such labels risks confirming the model's existing biases (a form of reward hacking), and the paper neither discusses nor controls for this failure mode, especially in the misaligned-initialization regime it acknowledges.

Missing statistical rigor: main results (Tables 2, 3) appear to be single runs without error bars or significance tests, despite LLM-judge evaluation noise (AlpacaEval 2) and reported seed variance elsewhere (Appendix H); some gaps over baseline are modest relative to this noise.

Internal consistency issues: the text claims RE-PO 'typically achieves the best performance' and 'consistently improves', yet Table 2 shows SimPO w/ LS beating RE-SimPO on Llama-3-8B LC (48.1 vs 46.9) and mixed results elsewhere; the strong 'consistently enhances' claims are stronger than the evidence. Also inconsistent naming in text ('R-DPO', 'HoldeRE-DPO') suggests insufficient proofreading.

The K=1 'virtual annotator' simplification (footnote 4) is under-justified: the marginalization-based confidence then depends on a single global η, reducing the method essentially to a dynamic label-smoothing schedule, and this simplification is exactly the configuration producing the headline numbers.
Significant hyperparameter sensitivity (η0 and α, Table 4) is reported without guidance on how to set them for new datasets/models, weakening practical applicability.

strengths: Addresses a real and practically important problem: label noise and annotator unreliability in preference data for LLM alignment, with clear motivation from prior empirical studies (20-40% corrupted pairs).

The EM formulation is clean and well-derived: the latent-variable model (Eqs. 3-6) follows standard Dawid-Skene-style reasoning, and the appendix provides a complete, careful derivation of the E-step, M-step, and closed-form reliability update (Appendices A-C).

The generalized probabilistic link between arbitrary preference losses and preference probabilities (Eq. 2) is a nice unifying device, and the paper verifies it recovers the Bradley-Terry model for DPO (Appendix B), supporting the 'general framework' claim across DPO/IPO/SimPO/CPO.

Broad and well-designed empirical evaluation: four alignment algorithms, two backbones, AlpacaEval 2 and Arena-Hard, a genuine multi-annotator dataset (MultiPref) with 227 annotators, robustness baselines (rDPO, Hölder-DPO, label smoothing), judge-model robustness check (Appendix G), runtime overhead analysis (Appendix H), and hyperparameter ablations (Section 5.4).

The paper is honest about theoretical limitations: Theorem 4.1 assumes a perfectly calibrated model, and Section 6 explicitly acknowledges this; Section 5.5 provides controlled synthetic-noise experiments that empirically validate the reliability-estimation claim.
Qualitative case studies (Appendix F) give concrete evidence that low-confidence examples correspond to genuinely noisy or reversed labels.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate rather than high: applying Dawid-Skene/Crowd-BT-style EM to preference optimization is a natural combination, and the space is already crowded (ROPO, rDPO, Hölder-DPO, Selective DPO). The delta over these prior robustness methods, beyond modeling annotator reliability explicitly, is not sharply articulated.

A significant mismatch between the method's core motivation and the main experiments: the UltraFeedback datasets used in the headline results (Table 2) contain no annotator identities, so the main experiments run with K=1 'virtual annotator'. In this regime, the confidence weights are derived almost entirely from the model's own posterior, raising a confirmation-bias concern: the model may systematically down-weight labels that disagree with its current (biased) preferences, and the paper does not analyze or ablate this risk.

The generalized probabilistic model (Eq. 2) is asserted to apply to 'any preference loss', but losses like IPO (squared loss) and SimPO do not obviously correspond to well-calibrated preference probabilities under this construction; the probabilistic validity for non-BT losses is not established beyond formal substitution.

Theoretical guarantees are quite idealized: convergence is proven only for the reliability parameter η under full-batch training with a perfectly calibrated, converged policy; the joint (θ, η) mini-batch dynamics—which is what is actually run—are not analyzed.

Statistical rigor is insufficient for the magnitude of claims: Tables 2 and 3 report single numbers with no error bars or seed variance (unlike the runtime appendix), and some gains are small or inconsistent (e.g., CPO on Mistral: RE-PO 27.6 LC vs. label smoothing 28.5; SimPO w/ LS 48.1 beats RE-PO 46.9 on Llama-3-8B), while AlpacaEval 2 LC differences of a few points are known to be noisy.
Only AlpacaEval 2 (and Arena-Hard in one ablation table) is used for evaluation; no human evaluation or complementary benchmarks (e.g., MT-Bench) to corroborate LLM-judge-based win rates.

Considerable hyperparameter sensitivity (η0 and α show swings of 3-5 points in the ablation), which implies a tuning burden not present in vanilla baselines; ablations are only run for one method-backbone pair (RE-DPO on Mistral).
No explicit statement of code release; given the many implementation details (EMA updates, initialization ranges, weighting application), reproducibility depends on this.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and well-motivated problem: label noise in preference data for LLM alignment.

The EM-based framework is cleanly derived, with complete E/M-step derivations, a general Boltzmann-style construction connecting preference losses to induced probabilistic models, and an honest discussion of where the induced objective diverges from the original loss (e.g., IPO, SimPO, CPO).

Experiments are reasonably broad: four alignment objectives (DPO, IPO, SimPO, CPO) across two backbones, comparison to label smoothing and two robust baselines (rDPO, Hölder-DPO), a real multi-annotator dataset (MultiPref) with 227 annotators, hyperparameter ablations, judge-model robustness checks, and runtime overhead measurements.

The controlled synthetic-noise experiments (Section 5.5, Figure 2) empirically support the reliability-identification claim, and Appendix E provides useful visualization of learned annotator reliabilities.
The paper is clearly written, with good reproducibility support (resource links, runtime details, code promised).
weaknesses: Limited novelty over prior work. The core mechanism — EM-style posterior re-weighting of noisy preference labels — is a direct combination of classic crowdsourcing ideas (Dawid–Skene, Crowd-BT) with DPO-style losses, and is very close to existing robust-preference methods the authors themselves cite (ROPO, rDPO, cDPO-style label smoothing). The 'general framework' contribution via the Gibbs/Boltzmann construction is largely a repackaging rather than a new technical insight.

The theoretical result (Theorem 4.1) is a mild extension of the classic Dawid–Skene fixed-point argument under an idealized assumption (perfectly calibrated θ held fixed). It provides no joint convergence guarantee for (θ, η), which is the practically relevant regime, and the authors admit the assumption may not hold in practice.

Identification concern: on the main UltraFeedback datasets there is effectively a single 'virtual' annotator (K=1). With K=1, the label-correctness posterior w_i is computed from the model's own preferences, making the method a self-referential re-weighting scheme with confirmation-bias risk (the model down-weights examples that disagree with it), and the latent variable is weakly identified. This weakens the noisy-annotator framing on the main benchmarks, where the 'annotator' is actually a single reward model (ArmoRM).

Empirical gains are mixed rather than uniformly positive: RE-PO sometimes loses to simple label smoothing (e.g., SimPO w/ LS on Llama-3-8B LC 48.1 vs 46.9), and improvements are modest for several families (IPO/CPO on Mistral). No statistical significance testing or seed variance is reported for the main results (seed variance appears only in the runtime appendix).

Evaluation relies exclusively on LLM-judge benchmarks (AlpacaEval 2, Arena-Hard); no human evaluation or alternative automatic metrics (e.g., MT-Bench), and the reliability-verification experiment uses GPT-4o labels as 'ground truth,' which introduces circularity.

Notable hyperparameter sensitivity: performance varies substantially with the EMA momentum α (e.g., 35.5 at α=0.1 vs ~30 at α=0.001/0.01 on LC), which raises tuning-cost and robustness concerns for practitioners; the headline gains may partially reflect favorable tuning.

The ablation and main experiments are confined to small/mid-size 7–8B instruct models on one data regime; the claimed generality would be more convincing with noise-controlled experiments on the main benchmarks (synthetic noise is only used for the small Qwen reliability study) and at least one larger model.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: robustness of direct alignment methods (DPO/IPO/SimPO/CPO) to noisy preference labels.

The experimental scope is reasonably broad: four alignment objectives, two backbones (Mistral-7B, Llama-3-8B), AlpacaEval 2 and Arena-Hard, plus a genuine multi-annotator dataset (MultiPref) with 227 annotators.
The comparison set includes relevant robustness baselines (label smoothing, rDPO, Hölder-DPO), which many papers in this space omit.
A nice controlled synthetic-noise experiment (Section 5.5, Figure 2) empirically verifies that the reliability estimates track ground truth under both single- and two-annotator settings.

Useful transparency artifacts: runtime overhead measurements (Appendix H), reliability histograms across priors and backbones (Appendix E), judge-model robustness check (Appendix G), qualitative case studies of down-weighted labels, and an LLM-usage disclosure.
The EM derivation (Appendix C) and the Bradley-Terry consistency check (Appendix B) are correct and clearly written.
weaknesses: Limited core novelty. The central idea is the classic Dawid-Skene/Crowd-BT EM machinery (1979/2013) applied as confidence weighting on top of existing DPO-family losses. Close prior work such as ROPO already proposes iterative confidence-based down-weighting for preference optimization; the paper's positioning as 'explicitly modeling the data-generating process' does not constitute a substantial methodological advance beyond combining known components.

The theoretical contribution is very weak relative to its framing. Theorem 4.1 assumes θ is fixed at a perfectly calibrated θ* and only proves that the scalar reliability updates converge to a fixed point of a population operator under full-batch EM. There is no joint analysis of θ and η, no convergence rate, no finite-sample or mini-batch guarantee, and no result connecting reliability recovery to downstream policy quality. This is essentially a fixed-point consistency argument, not a meaningful guarantee for the actual algorithm.

The Boltzmann/Gibbs construction (Eq. 2) that 'lifts' the method to a general framework is ad hoc for non-likelihood losses (IPO, CPO). The paper admits the induced probability differs from the original objective for these losses, yet presents RE-IPO/RE-CPO as principled instances of the framework rather than as heuristic weighted variants. Notably, the qualitative analysis in Appendix F shows RE-PO down-weights 'labels inconsistent with the model's own predictions,' which raises the concern that the method reinforces model bias (confirmation dynamics) rather than genuinely denoising — a risk the theory does not address.

Evaluation issues undermine the headline claims: (i) no error bars, seeds, or significance tests for the main Table 2 results, while AlpacaEval 2 LC differences of 1–3 points are within known judge variance; the 'up to 7.0%' claim is a best-case (cherry-picked) cell; (ii) results are mixed — label smoothing beats RE-PO on SimPO/Llama LC (48.1 vs 46.9) and several RE-PO gains are marginal (CPO Mistral 26.3→27.6), so 'generally enhancing' overstates the evidence; (iii) the ablation's optimal hyperparameters (η0=0.9, α=0.1, marked 'Ours') were evidently selected on the same evaluation benchmark, and Table 4 shows the method is quite sensitive to α, raising winner's-curse concerns.

The main experiments (UltraFeedback) use a single virtual annotator (K=1), collapsing the annotator-reliability model to a single scalar; the framework's distinguishing feature (per-annotator reliability) is only exercised in the smaller MultiPref/DPO-only study, which also lacks the label-smoothing and rDPO/Hölder-DPO baselines.

Presentation/complete-submission issues: the abstract ends mid-sentence ('Our code and other resources are available at'), the reproducbility statement is similarly truncated, and Arena-Hard results appear only in an ablation table for one configuration rather than as a systematic evaluation.

The gap between the idealized theory (perfect calibration) and practice is acknowledged but not resolved; there is no analysis or experiment demonstrating behavior under a genuinely misaligned base model, which is exactly the regime where confidence-based self-weighting is known to fail.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical problem: noise in preference data used for LLM alignment, and proposes a principled EM-based framework that treats label correctness and annotator reliability as latent variables, connecting to the well-established Dawid–Skene / Crowd-BT lineage.

The generalized formulation via a Boltzmann/Gibbs construction (Eq. 2) that maps a broad class of preference losses to induced probabilistic models is elegant, and the derivation showing DPO recovers the Bradley–Terry model (Appendix B) is clean and correct.

The theoretical result (Theorem 4.1) is clearly stated, honestly framed as idealized (perfect calibration, full-batch), with a correct population-level proof in Appendix D, and is backed by a dedicated empirical verification section (5.5) with controlled synthetic noise experiments.

The experimental evaluation is comprehensive: four preference objectives (DPO, IPO, SimPO, CPO), two backbones, comparisons against both natural baselines (label smoothing) and specialized robust methods (rDPO, Hölder-DPO), a real multi-annotator dataset (MultiPref) with 227 annotators where the per-annotator mechanism is genuinely exercised, hyperparameter ablations, judge-model robustness checks (Appendix G), and runtime overhead analysis (Table 8).

Reproducibility is well supported: public datasets/models, implementation details, resource links, runtime measurements, and a code repository; reported gains (up to +7 LC points) are meaningful on AlpacaEval 2 and consistent on MultiPref and with an alternate judge (DeepSeek).
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: EM-based per-sample reweighting with annotator reliability modeling is a well-trodden technique (Dawid–Skene 1979, Crowd-BT 2013), and several closely related robust DPO variants already exist (ROPO, rDPO, Hölder-DPO). The paper's core contribution is a natural combination of these ideas with preference optimization; ROPO in particular is claimed to be complementary but is not compared empirically.

In the main experiments (Table 2), the UltraFeedback datasets are treated as coming from a single virtual annotator (K=1), which significantly undercuts the framework's distinguishing feature (per-annotator reliability modeling); with K=1 the method largely reduces to adaptive per-sample soft weighting, and the effective-reliability justification in footnote 2 is heuristic.

Results are not uniformly positive: for CPO on Mistral-7B the label-smoothing baseline outperforms RE-PO, and for SimPO on Llama-3-8B label smoothing achieves the best LC (48.1 vs. 46.9). The claim that RE-PO 'generally enhances' the baselines is accurate but weaker than the abstract implies, and no error bars or significance tests are reported for the main results (only runtime uses multiple seeds).

The theoretical guarantee relies on a perfectly calibrated policy, which is the key assumption; the practical gap is acknowledged but only partially mitigated empirically. The related circularity concern—that confidence weights come from a model trained on the same noisy labels, risking self-reinforcing confirmation bias—is not deeply analyzed.

Theorem 4.1 concerns only the reliability η update under a fixed, converged policy; there is no analysis of the joint dynamics of θ and η, and the practical procedure (mini-batch, EMA, single-epoch training) deviates substantially from the idealized full-batch EM assumed in the theory.

Ablations are limited to a single method/backbone (RE-DPO on Mistral-7B), and the method shows considerable sensitivity to the EMA momentum α, raising generalization concerns about the reported optimal hyperparameters across other settings.

Evaluation relies almost entirely on LLM-judge benchmarks (AlpacaEval 2, Arena-Hard in ablation only); no human evaluation or non-judge-based metrics are provided, which is a limitation for a paper whose central claim is about the quality of learned preferences.
